gap.reason: The introduction identifies a material-performance tradeoff: MM’X alloys need improved mechanical integrity while retaining a large magnetocaloric effect, motivating the design of new magnetocaloric high-entropy alloys.

source_text:
Solid-state refrigeration technology is a new type of refrigeration technology with the advantages of environmental protection, energy savings, high efficiency, stability, and reliability. It is feasibly regarded as the next generation of refrigeration technology by the United States Department of Energy. Solid-state refrigeration technologies are mainly divided into magnetic refrigeration technology, thermoelectric refrigeration technology, and mechanical thermal refrigeration technology, including multicaloric refrigeration by multiple fields (magnetic fields, pressure fields, electric fields, etc.). The magnetocaloric effect (MCE) seen when using magnetic materials as the working medium, exhibiting very low levels of energy consumption, is the basic principle of magnetic refrigeration. The working efficiency of magnetic refrigeration can reach 30–60% of the Carnot cycle, which is much higher than that of the vapor compression refrigeration and several other solid-state refrigeration technologies. Hence, magnetic refrigeration is widely considered to be the next generation of refrigeration technology with a wide operating temperature range, stable operation without noise, and long service life.

MnNiSi-based magnetic refrigeration materials have attracted more and more attention from researchers because of the large magnetocaloric effect and wide adjustable Curie temperature window (CTW) effect. These alloys families exhibit a martensitic-like phase transition from Ni2In-type structure to TiNiSi-type structure, and the transformation process is accompanied by giant negative thermal expansion. However, the poor mechanical properties induced by a severe first-order phase transition (FOPT) hinder the commercialization of MnNiSi-based alloys. For example, the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 HEA, which struggles to maintain its integrity due to poor mechanical properties, shows giant caloric effect under magnetic field and pressure field. Giant changes in crystal structure and internal stress of these types of alloys induced by drastic first-order phase transformation will cause the alloys to tend to crack and lead to the deterioration of its mechanical properties. Several researchers have worked extensively to solve this problem. F. Zhu et al. improved the mechanical properties of Mn0.98CoGe alloy by epoxy bonding. They found that the compression strength of the alloy reached 152 MPa when the epoxy resin content was 3 wt.% and 218 MPa when it was 5 wt.%. H. Zhou et al. prepared low-melting metal-bonded MM’X/In composites to improve mechanical properties. The compressive strength of the alloy with 25 wt.% In reached 48 MPa. When the In content was 30 wt.%, the thermal conductivity of the alloy was enhanced by more than 8 times compared to the samples bonded with epoxy resin. They believe this results from the low-porosity compact structure formed by the high ductility of In, which greatly improved the mechanical properties and thermal conductivity of the alloy.

Recently, more and more researchers have paid attention to high-entropy alloys (HEAs) due to their outstanding mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, radiation resistance, and low-temperature performance. There are generally two definitions of HEAs. From the perspective of mixing and phase formation, the mixing entropy of high-entropy alloy systems is very high, which is composed of configurational entropy, magnetic entropy, vibrational entropy, and electronic entropy. Out of these, configurational entropy is the most important factor. Therefore, alloys can be distinguished into low-entropy alloys (∆Sconf<1R), medium-entropy alloy (1R ≤∆Sconf≤1.5R), and high-entropy alloys (∆Sconf>1.5R) according to the configuration entropy. Meanwhile, HEAs are defined as alloys with five or more elements. Each major element is of 5–35 at%, while the content of each minor element is less than 5 at%. As an important direction of functional HEAs, the published works on magnetocaloric high-entropy alloys (MCE-HEAs) are less than 0.5% of the total HEA research, while most MCE-HEAs exhibiting giant magnetocaloric effects include rare-earth-based elements. It was reported that (FeMnNi)66.7(Ge0.45Si0.55)33.3 exhibited a giant isothermal entropy change of 13 J∙kg−1K−1 at 2.5 T, which was comparable to the notable MCE-HEAs Gd20Dy20Er20Ho20Tb20 (isothermal entropy change of8.6 J∙kg−1K−1 at 5 T). More MCE-HEAs of rare-earth-free (RE-free) show surprising magnetocaloric effects, which indicated that RE-free HEAs have great research potential when applied for refrigeration. However, it is a problem that great magnetocaloric effects are generally accompanied by limited mechanical properties in MM’X magnetocaloric materials. An ideal combination of great MCE and mechanical properties would be achieved by designing the magnetocaloric materials as high-entropy alloys. Therefore, it is worthwhile exploring the potential application of new magnetocaloric high-entropy alloys.

We previously discussed the effect of the Si/Ge ratio on MM’X alloys in the published article.

queries.broad: For MnNiSi-based magnetic-refrigeration materials, what single intervention could improve mechanical performance while retaining a large magnetocaloric effect? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected changes relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.
queries.problem_constrained: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibits a giant caloric effect under magnetic and pressure fields but struggles to maintain its integrity because the severe first-order phase transition produces large crystal-structure changes and internal stress that promote cracking. What single intervention could improve its mechanical integrity while preserving its caloric performance under the relevant field-driven operating regime? State the proposed mechanism, predicted mechanical and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.
queries.expert_context: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibits a giant caloric effect under magnetic and pressure fields but has poor integrity because its severe first-order phase transition generates large structural changes, internal stress, and cracking. Earlier work used epoxy bonding in Mn0.98CoGe, reporting compressive strengths of 152 MPa at 3 wt.% epoxy and 218 MPa at 5 wt.%, while low-melting In bonding in MM′X composites produced 48 MPa compressive strength at 25 wt.% In and, at 30 wt.% In, more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-bonded samples; these approaches improved selected mechanical or transport metrics, but the ideal combination of strong magnetocaloric response and mechanical properties remains unresolved. Rare-earth-free magnetocaloric high-entropy alloys are of particular interest, with high-entropy character defined either by configurational entropy above 1.5R or by at least five major elements at 5–35 at.% each, with minor elements below 5 at.%. Given these constraints, what single intervention could improve the starting alloy’s mechanical integrity without sacrificing its caloric response under magnetic- and pressure-field operation? Present one hypothesis containing the intervention, mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment that would falsify it.

queries.problem_constrained: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.
queries.expert_context: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.
